concept.name: Daily settlement price
concept.definition: The official daily price at which the clearing organization clears all trades and settles all accounts between clearing members for each contract month; it is the benchmark used for marking positions to market, computing margin calls, and invoicing deliveries.
concept.intuition: The daily settlement price is the exchange's official 'score' for the day: everyone's futures P&L and margin requirements are recomputed against it every session.
concept.mechanics: Exchanges derive it from trading activity near the close (e.g., a volume-weighted average over a designated closing period, with exchange discretion in illiquid conditions). All open positions are marked to this price daily: gains are credited and losses debited (variation margin), and for physically delivered contracts it feeds the delivery invoice price.
concept.failure_modes: In illiquid or disorderly closes the settlement price may differ from the last trade, so P&L and margin calls can move against a trader even when their executed prices looked favorable; it is also a manipulation target ('banging the close').
concept.misconceptions: The settlement price is not necessarily the last traded price or the simple closing quote — exchanges use defined closing-period procedures; and daily price limits are measured against the prior day's settlement, not the last trade.
concept.example: If yesterday's settle on a corn future was 450 cents and today's settle is 460, a long one-contract position is credited 10 cents x 5,000 bushels = $500 of variation margin overnight.
